medical.title: Achilles injections show no meaningful benefit over sham treatment
medical.summary: Commonly used injections for Achilles tendinopathy—pain, stiffness and swelling in the Achilles tendon—offer no meaningful clinical advantage over placebo (sham) treatment, finds a clinical trial published by The BMJ.

medical.title: Wider surgical margins may not mean better cancer control
medical.summary: It's a question that surgeons often face: How much surrounding healthy tissue should they take out when removing a patient's cancer to be sure it is fully eliminated? Removing more can sacrifice nearby nerves, blood vessels, tendons and even joints, with lasting effects on quality of life.

medical.title: Smoke from LA fires exposed millions of people to high levels of toxic heavy metals, study says
medical.summary: At the height of the Los Angeles fires in 2025, millions of residents were exposed in a 24-hour period to toxic lead levels from smoke that were 80 times higher than the typical background level, according to a new study.

medical.title: Mutated immune cells raise red flags in lupus
medical.summary: Scientists at La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) and the University of Washington (UW) have discovered that patients with lupus have unusual mutations that may turn their bodies into battlegrounds.

medical.title: How sex-based biology shapes the brain's response to injury
medical.summary: Injury-induced stress cascades through the body by activating immune responses, shifting energy away from less urgent concerns to prioritize healing. In traumatic brain injury, or TBI, the brain—home to the signaling hubs that manage those safety processes—is the site of the incident.

medical.title: Deep brain stimulation in patients with epilepsy produces measurable response within minutes, study finds
medical.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers have detected measurable changes in the brain within 18 minutes of deep brain stimulation (DBS) in people with drug-resistant epilepsy, a finding that could eventually help clinicians personalize treatment without waiting months to determine whether stimulation settings are effective. The study was recently published in iScience.

medical.title: New microscopy platform enables imaging of neuronal activity at single-cell resolution at unprecedented tissue depth
medical.summary: As light travels deeper into the brain, it scatters. Three-photon microscopy, the current state of the art, reduces the resulting background fluorescence and can, in principle, image much deeper than earlier techniques—but to do that, it uses average laser power limits that cause overheating and damage living tissue.

medical.title: Living near water-pollution sources associated with rare brain disorder
medical.summary: People who live near industrial facilities that pollute the water supply may be more likely to develop a rare movement disorder called progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), according to a study published in Neurology.

science.title: Ultrathin metal layer boosts spin-related signals, opening a door to ultralow-power electronics
science.summary: Researchers at Kyushu University have found that an ultrathin layer of iridium manganese (IrMn) can improve two spin-related signals in a structure made of a magnetic insulator and a platinum film. By examining how spin currents are generated and absorbed, the team gained insights into how the intermediate layer improves spin transfer. The findings could inform the development of ultralow-power devices for computing and energy harvesting.

science.title: Atomic magnetism reveals why iron, but not chromium, can produce ammonia using sunlight
science.summary: Two nearly identical materials have completely different chemical behavior. Research teams at the University of Vienna and TU Wien studied catalysts that use the energy of sunlight to produce ammonia. Surprisingly, when the three iron atoms that form tiny triangles in these catalysts are replaced by chromium atoms, the chemical reaction no longer takes place.

science.title: Macromolecular crowding could help build artificial cell systems
science.summary: Macromolecular crowding can serve as a design tool for controlling the formation and organization of synthetic DNA droplets, a study from Science Tokyo reveals. Researchers investigated this strategy using DNA nanostars and polymeric crowding agents to mimic the crowded cellular environment. They found that crowding promoted droplet formation and enabled control over droplet size, interactions and organization. The findings could support the development of programmable artificial cell systems.

science.title: Molecular architecture determines tomato plant resistance to its main pest
science.summary: An international study investigating why wild tomatoes are more resistant to the tomato leafminer (Phthorimaea absoluta) than cultivated varieties revealed that the secret lies in the spatial structure of a plant defense molecule. The researchers mapped the biochemical origin of this difference and demonstrated that altering four amino acids in a single enzyme is sufficient to alter the structure of the substance and increase its toxicity against the pest. This finding paves the way for creating resistant tomatoes through gene editing.

science.title: Explaining the difference between brittle and ductile behavior in polymer glasses
science.summary: Glasses are (mostly) brittle, metals can be ductile (plastic), and liquids flow easily. Polymers are interesting because they exhibit all three types of behavior, depending on their chemical nature, temperature, and deformation rate. If polymers are not able to crystallize, their low-temperature state is glassy, and they are hard and transparent. One example is poly(methylmethacrylate) [PMMA], which has been used as an artificial glass since the early 20th century.

science.title: NASA Welcomes Vietnam as Newest Artemis Accords Signatory
science.summary: The Socialist Republic of Vietnam became the 78th nation to sign the Artemis Accords, joining a growing coalition of like-minded nations committed to the peaceful, transparent, and responsible exploration of space.   “Vietnam is joining at an important point in the development of its own space program,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson in recorded remarks […]

science.title: Q&A: Decoding the cell—a conversation with a computational biologist
science.summary: Computational biologist Christina Leslie, Ph.D., has spent nearly two decades at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) building computational tools that help make sense of some of the most complex data in biology.

science.title: Chornobyl dog population shows genetic signatures of directional selection
science.summary: The latest research on the wild population of dogs in Chornobyl reveals that the genetic differences between these dogs and other similarly isolated dog populations are likely evidence of directional selection, not mutation. The work suggests a potential association between genetic selection and environmental variables and could advance understanding of local adaptation and genomic resilience in contaminated environments. The study appears in Genes.

science.title: Could next-gen artificial intelligence help map out future space outposts?
science.summary: Planning a successful trip can be challenging, especially when your destination is in outer space. Even before liftoff, space missions require extraordinary amounts of scientific preparation and data analysis to succeed, which can take years to complete. However, as space agencies race to establish a permanent presence on the moon, using artificial intelligence to combine such information into a single system could make mission planning much more efficient.

science.title: Same radical, different paths: X-ray snapshots reveal how neighboring molecules shape its movement
science.summary: Chemical reactions have their own "impatient molecules." Unable to stay still even for a moment, they latch onto other molecules indiscriminately. Researchers have now found that even these molecules change where they "sit" and how far they roam depending on who their neighbors are. The findings are expected to help scientists make better medicines and materials by directing reactions only to the desired sites.

science.title: Rarely seen deep-sea barreleye fish filmed in 4K
science.summary: During a recent expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard, MBARI scientists encountered a rarely seen barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma). This sighting is MBARI's 11th observation of this unique deep-sea fish with a transparent head.

science.title: Drones could help weather forecasters more accurately predict winter storms
science.summary: Weather drones are being tested to help update forecasts of extreme weather more quickly, and could help us prepare earlier for upcoming winter storms.

science.title: Controlling where gibberellin acts reveals how the plant hormone coordinates root growth
science.summary: Plant hormones influence growth and development by acting on specific cells and tissues. However, determining precisely where and when a hormone needs to act has been challenging because conventional hormone treatment generally activates signaling throughout the plant.

science.title: 150-year-old mystery about the identity of an 'extinct' giant crane solved
science.summary: Scientists at Bournemouth University (BU) have solved a 150-year-old mystery about the identity of an extinct giant crane that lived in Europe over 20,000 years ago. The work is published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

science.title: Relocating amphibians and reptiles to make way for human development rarely delivers long-term conservation success
science.summary: Relocating amphibians and reptiles to protect them from development rarely leads to long-term conservation success, a new UBC-led global review has found. The findings highlight the importance of habitat protection rather than relying on moving animals out of harm's way.

science.title: Customizable DNA labels can selectively guide drug carriers to cancer cells
science.summary: Cells naturally send tiny packages to one another to share information. Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University have developed a simple, low-cost way to turn those packages into drug carriers that can deliver treatments directly to cancer cells, potentially improving effectiveness while reducing side effects.

environment.title: Suriname’s rich archaeological history may hold keys to conservation
environment.summary: Suriname pledges to save its forests but neglects the ancient human history hidden within them, experts say.

environment.title: A town-wide ‘living laboratory’ shows how green spaces can combat climate extremes
environment.summary: Stoke Park is a natural haven in a busy British town. Centered in Guildford, Surrey, its rolling fields pop with wildflowers in the spring; birds sing and ducks paddle serenely in a pond beside ornamental gardens; and the sun casts dappled shade on the grass from oak, spruce and beech trees, scattered across 52 hectares […]

environment.title: Why I sent my archive of nature’s sounds to France (commentary)
environment.summary: It is a peculiar irony: as technology reaches ever deeper into Earth’s living systems, the primal sonic expressions of the natural world—wind, water, leaf, and creature—have never been more imperiled. Soundscape ecology rests on a simple conviction: the collective voices of the nonhuman world are not only eloquent, but essential. Recorded and preserved over time, […]

environment.title: US public lands tracker highlights the collective impact of Trump policies
environment.summary: In his second term as the U.S. president, Donald Trump has taken actions to remove protections from at least 34.8 million hectares (86 million acres) of public lands, according to the advocacy group Center for American Progress. The nonprofit Conservation Lands Foundation (CLF) recently catalogued 12 such policy actions in its newly released Public Lands […]

environment.title: Cyclone batters India’s eastern coast, killing 3 and damaging homes and farmland
environment.summary: KAKINADA, India (AP) — A powerful cyclone battered India ’s Andhra Pradesh state on Wednesday, killing at least three people and damaging homes and farmland after authorities evacuated tens of thousands of people, officials said. Cyclone Arnab made landfall early Wednesday as a very severe cyclonic storm before weakening to a severe cyclonic storm as […]

environment.title: Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years
environment.summary: Switzerland’s glaciers are disappearing at an alarming rate, losing more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Some of the country’s most famous glaciers experienced their worst melting on record, while several smaller glaciers vanished completely. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.

environment.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in Japan's 7,300-year-old volcanic apocalypse
environment.summary: A catastrophic volcanic eruption 7,300 years ago devastated Japan, but new research reveals that its impact on prehistoric populations was far more complex than previously believed. While some communities disappeared or declined, others unexpectedly flourished as survivors migrated, adapted, and found new ways to thrive.

environment.title: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
environment.summary: Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.

environment.title: Europe's new Sentinel-3C satellite just sent back spectacular images of Earth
environment.summary: Europe's Sentinel-3C satellite has returned breathtaking images of Earth just two weeks after launch, revealing the snowy Alps, frozen Arctic islands, and brilliant turquoise Caribbean waters. Its first measurements also show promising results for tracking rising seas, melting ice sheets, and other changes reshaping our planet.

environment.title: Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
environment.summary: Scientists may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth maintained enough oxygen to support life. Ancient rocks reveal that phosphorus recycling in the oceans created a self-sustaining cycle that helped keep oxygen levels high, even as the planet underwent dramatic environmental changes. The discovery challenges assumptions about Earth's early atmosphere and raises new questions about why complex life took so long to emerge.

environment.title: Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
environment.summary: The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. Scientists discovered that these changes in the genome's 3D structure may have helped drive the evolution of their unusually complex nervous systems.

mix_items.title: Ultrathin metal layer boosts spin-related signals, opening a door to ultralow-power electronics
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Kyushu University have found that an ultrathin layer of iridium manganese (IrMn) can improve two spin-related signals in a structure made of a magnetic insulator and a platinum film. By examining how spin currents are generated and absorbed, the team gained insights into how the intermediate layer improves spin transfer. The findings could inform the development of ultralow-power devices for computing and energy harvesting.

mix_items.title: Atomic magnetism reveals why iron, but not chromium, can produce ammonia using sunlight
mix_items.summary: Two nearly identical materials have completely different chemical behavior. Research teams at the University of Vienna and TU Wien studied catalysts that use the energy of sunlight to produce ammonia. Surprisingly, when the three iron atoms that form tiny triangles in these catalysts are replaced by chromium atoms, the chemical reaction no longer takes place.

mix_items.title: Macromolecular crowding could help build artificial cell systems
mix_items.summary: Macromolecular crowding can serve as a design tool for controlling the formation and organization of synthetic DNA droplets, a study from Science Tokyo reveals. Researchers investigated this strategy using DNA nanostars and polymeric crowding agents to mimic the crowded cellular environment. They found that crowding promoted droplet formation and enabled control over droplet size, interactions and organization. The findings could support the development of programmable artificial cell systems.

mix_items.title: Achilles injections show no meaningful benefit over sham treatment
mix_items.summary: Commonly used injections for Achilles tendinopathy—pain, stiffness and swelling in the Achilles tendon—offer no meaningful clinical advantage over placebo (sham) treatment, finds a clinical trial published by The BMJ.

mix_items.title: Molecular architecture determines tomato plant resistance to its main pest
mix_items.summary: An international study investigating why wild tomatoes are more resistant to the tomato leafminer (Phthorimaea absoluta) than cultivated varieties revealed that the secret lies in the spatial structure of a plant defense molecule. The researchers mapped the biochemical origin of this difference and demonstrated that altering four amino acids in a single enzyme is sufficient to alter the structure of the substance and increase its toxicity against the pest. This finding paves the way for creating resistant tomatoes through gene editing.

mix_items.title: Wider surgical margins may not mean better cancer control
mix_items.summary: It's a question that surgeons often face: How much surrounding healthy tissue should they take out when removing a patient's cancer to be sure it is fully eliminated? Removing more can sacrifice nearby nerves, blood vessels, tendons and even joints, with lasting effects on quality of life.

mix_items.title: Smoke from LA fires exposed millions of people to high levels of toxic heavy metals, study says
mix_items.summary: At the height of the Los Angeles fires in 2025, millions of residents were exposed in a 24-hour period to toxic lead levels from smoke that were 80 times higher than the typical background level, according to a new study.

mix_items.title: Mutated immune cells raise red flags in lupus
mix_items.summary: Scientists at La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) and the University of Washington (UW) have discovered that patients with lupus have unusual mutations that may turn their bodies into battlegrounds.

mix_items.title: Explaining the difference between brittle and ductile behavior in polymer glasses
mix_items.summary: Glasses are (mostly) brittle, metals can be ductile (plastic), and liquids flow easily. Polymers are interesting because they exhibit all three types of behavior, depending on their chemical nature, temperature, and deformation rate. If polymers are not able to crystallize, their low-temperature state is glassy, and they are hard and transparent. One example is poly(methylmethacrylate) [PMMA], which has been used as an artificial glass since the early 20th century.

mix_items.title: NASA Welcomes Vietnam as Newest Artemis Accords Signatory
mix_items.summary: The Socialist Republic of Vietnam became the 78th nation to sign the Artemis Accords, joining a growing coalition of like-minded nations committed to the peaceful, transparent, and responsible exploration of space.   “Vietnam is joining at an important point in the development of its own space program,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson in recorded remarks […]

mix_items.title: Q&A: Decoding the cell—a conversation with a computational biologist
mix_items.summary: Computational biologist Christina Leslie, Ph.D., has spent nearly two decades at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) building computational tools that help make sense of some of the most complex data in biology.

mix_items.title: Chornobyl dog population shows genetic signatures of directional selection
mix_items.summary: The latest research on the wild population of dogs in Chornobyl reveals that the genetic differences between these dogs and other similarly isolated dog populations are likely evidence of directional selection, not mutation. The work suggests a potential association between genetic selection and environmental variables and could advance understanding of local adaptation and genomic resilience in contaminated environments. The study appears in Genes.

mix_items.title: Could next-gen artificial intelligence help map out future space outposts?
mix_items.summary: Planning a successful trip can be challenging, especially when your destination is in outer space. Even before liftoff, space missions require extraordinary amounts of scientific preparation and data analysis to succeed, which can take years to complete. However, as space agencies race to establish a permanent presence on the moon, using artificial intelligence to combine such information into a single system could make mission planning much more efficient.

mix_items.title: Same radical, different paths: X-ray snapshots reveal how neighboring molecules shape its movement
mix_items.summary: Chemical reactions have their own "impatient molecules." Unable to stay still even for a moment, they latch onto other molecules indiscriminately. Researchers have now found that even these molecules change where they "sit" and how far they roam depending on who their neighbors are. The findings are expected to help scientists make better medicines and materials by directing reactions only to the desired sites.

mix_items.title: Rarely seen deep-sea barreleye fish filmed in 4K
mix_items.summary: During a recent expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard, MBARI scientists encountered a rarely seen barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma). This sighting is MBARI's 11th observation of this unique deep-sea fish with a transparent head.

mix_items.title: Drones could help weather forecasters more accurately predict winter storms
mix_items.summary: Weather drones are being tested to help update forecasts of extreme weather more quickly, and could help us prepare earlier for upcoming winter storms.

mix_items.title: Controlling where gibberellin acts reveals how the plant hormone coordinates root growth
mix_items.summary: Plant hormones influence growth and development by acting on specific cells and tissues. However, determining precisely where and when a hormone needs to act has been challenging because conventional hormone treatment generally activates signaling throughout the plant.

mix_items.title: How sex-based biology shapes the brain's response to injury
mix_items.summary: Injury-induced stress cascades through the body by activating immune responses, shifting energy away from less urgent concerns to prioritize healing. In traumatic brain injury, or TBI, the brain—home to the signaling hubs that manage those safety processes—is the site of the incident.

mix_items.title: Deep brain stimulation in patients with epilepsy produces measurable response within minutes, study finds
mix_items.summary: Mayo Clinic researchers have detected measurable changes in the brain within 18 minutes of deep brain stimulation (DBS) in people with drug-resistant epilepsy, a finding that could eventually help clinicians personalize treatment without waiting months to determine whether stimulation settings are effective. The study was recently published in iScience.

mix_items.title: 150-year-old mystery about the identity of an 'extinct' giant crane solved
mix_items.summary: Scientists at Bournemouth University (BU) have solved a 150-year-old mystery about the identity of an extinct giant crane that lived in Europe over 20,000 years ago. The work is published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

mix_items.title: Relocating amphibians and reptiles to make way for human development rarely delivers long-term conservation success
mix_items.summary: Relocating amphibians and reptiles to protect them from development rarely leads to long-term conservation success, a new UBC-led global review has found. The findings highlight the importance of habitat protection rather than relying on moving animals out of harm's way.

mix_items.title: New microscopy platform enables imaging of neuronal activity at single-cell resolution at unprecedented tissue depth
mix_items.summary: As light travels deeper into the brain, it scatters. Three-photon microscopy, the current state of the art, reduces the resulting background fluorescence and can, in principle, image much deeper than earlier techniques—but to do that, it uses average laser power limits that cause overheating and damage living tissue.

mix_items.title: Customizable DNA labels can selectively guide drug carriers to cancer cells
mix_items.summary: Cells naturally send tiny packages to one another to share information. Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University have developed a simple, low-cost way to turn those packages into drug carriers that can deliver treatments directly to cancer cells, potentially improving effectiveness while reducing side effects.

mix_items.title: Living near water-pollution sources associated with rare brain disorder
mix_items.summary: People who live near industrial facilities that pollute the water supply may be more likely to develop a rare movement disorder called progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), according to a study published in Neurology.

mix_items.title: Suriname’s rich archaeological history may hold keys to conservation
mix_items.summary: Suriname pledges to save its forests but neglects the ancient human history hidden within them, experts say.

mix_items.title: A town-wide ‘living laboratory’ shows how green spaces can combat climate extremes
mix_items.summary: Stoke Park is a natural haven in a busy British town. Centered in Guildford, Surrey, its rolling fields pop with wildflowers in the spring; birds sing and ducks paddle serenely in a pond beside ornamental gardens; and the sun casts dappled shade on the grass from oak, spruce and beech trees, scattered across 52 hectares […]

mix_items.title: Why I sent my archive of nature’s sounds to France (commentary)
mix_items.summary: It is a peculiar irony: as technology reaches ever deeper into Earth’s living systems, the primal sonic expressions of the natural world—wind, water, leaf, and creature—have never been more imperiled. Soundscape ecology rests on a simple conviction: the collective voices of the nonhuman world are not only eloquent, but essential. Recorded and preserved over time, […]

mix_items.title: US public lands tracker highlights the collective impact of Trump policies
mix_items.summary: In his second term as the U.S. president, Donald Trump has taken actions to remove protections from at least 34.8 million hectares (86 million acres) of public lands, according to the advocacy group Center for American Progress. The nonprofit Conservation Lands Foundation (CLF) recently catalogued 12 such policy actions in its newly released Public Lands […]

mix_items.title: Cyclone batters India’s eastern coast, killing 3 and damaging homes and farmland
mix_items.summary: KAKINADA, India (AP) — A powerful cyclone battered India ’s Andhra Pradesh state on Wednesday, killing at least three people and damaging homes and farmland after authorities evacuated tens of thousands of people, officials said. Cyclone Arnab made landfall early Wednesday as a very severe cyclonic storm before weakening to a severe cyclonic storm as […]

mix_items.title: Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has vanished in just five years
mix_items.summary: Switzerland’s glaciers are disappearing at an alarming rate, losing more than 5% of their ice volume in 2026 alone. Some of the country’s most famous glaciers experienced their worst melting on record, while several smaller glaciers vanished completely. Nearly 20% of Switzerland’s glacier ice has disappeared in just five years, driven by unusually snowless winters and extreme summer heat.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in Japan's 7,300-year-old volcanic apocalypse
mix_items.summary: A catastrophic volcanic eruption 7,300 years ago devastated Japan, but new research reveals that its impact on prehistoric populations was far more complex than previously believed. While some communities disappeared or declined, others unexpectedly flourished as survivors migrated, adapted, and found new ways to thrive.

mix_items.title: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
mix_items.summary: Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.

mix_items.title: Europe's new Sentinel-3C satellite just sent back spectacular images of Earth
mix_items.summary: Europe's Sentinel-3C satellite has returned breathtaking images of Earth just two weeks after launch, revealing the snowy Alps, frozen Arctic islands, and brilliant turquoise Caribbean waters. Its first measurements also show promising results for tracking rising seas, melting ice sheets, and other changes reshaping our planet.

mix_items.title: Scientists uncover the 2.3-billion-year-old secret that helped keep Earth habitable
mix_items.summary: Scientists may have solved a 2.3-billion-year-old mystery about how Earth maintained enough oxygen to support life. Ancient rocks reveal that phosphorus recycling in the oceans created a self-sustaining cycle that helped keep oxygen levels high, even as the planet underwent dramatic environmental changes. The discovery challenges assumptions about Earth's early atmosphere and raises new questions about why complex life took so long to emerge.

mix_items.title: Scientists find a surprising genetic twist behind octopus intelligence
mix_items.summary: The remarkable intelligence of octopuses, squid, and cuttlefish may trace back to an ancient reshuffling of their DNA that created new connections between genes. Scientists discovered that these changes in the genome's 3D structure may have helped drive the evolution of their unusually complex nervous systems.
